platforms.name: Cursor (tier: watching)
details: **Rollouts** — a new production-monitoring bot. It attaches a monitor to every pull request, reads the diff and the systems it touches, and writes a monitoring plan as a PR comment. It wakes on deploy events for the change's commit and runs that plan against the customer's logs, metrics and traces, tracking each environment separately and returning a per-environment verdict (verified healthy / regression detected / inconclusive). On a regression it names the suspected change, notifies the author, and — depending on configuration — **opens a revert PR or hands the finding to a cloud agent for a fix**. Integrations: source control (GitHub/Origin), the customer's CD system, and telemetry providers including Datadog, Grafana and Honeycomb. Teams and Enterprise plans. Source: https://cursor.com/changelog/rollouts-and-security-reviewer

**Security Review** — a new security-agent family shipped alongside Rollouts. *Security Reviewer* reads every pull request in the context of the whole codebase and posts a single review comment reporting exploitable bugs (SQL/command/template injection, authn/authz bypass, secrets and credentials, SSRF, unsafe deserialization, vulnerable dependencies). A companion *Vulnerability Scanner* scans the codebase **at rest** for pre-existing issues. Teams can add custom codebase rules. Enabled per repository from the dashboard; draft PRs excluded. Source: https://cursor.com/docs/security-agents

platforms.name: Google Gemini Enterprise (tier: secondary)
details: **D&B Finance Analytics data store (Public Preview)** — new third-party data store. Beyond read access to company and credit reports, scores, filings and corporate ownership, it **supports actions**: creating and processing credit applications, and managing folders. This is the fifth connector-action expansion since 2026-08-21 and the second D&B data store in three days (D&B Risk Analytics GA'd 2026-09-22). Source: https://docs.cloud.google.com/gemini/enterprise/docs/connectors/d-and-b-commercial-graph

platforms.name: Amazon Bedrock AgentCore (tier: primary) — carried audit debt cleared
details: **Caller-controlled model configuration and skill sources.** The `model.additionalParams`, `apiBase` and `modelId` fields on `InvokeHarness` are passed through to the model provider **unvalidated and unfiltered** by AWS. The `skills` field can be overridden per invocation to point the harness at arbitrary S3 or Git sources, and the harness "treats all skill content as trusted input." Source: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock-agentcore/latest/devguide/harness-security.html

**Harness IAM permission model and `harness-endpoint` resource type.** Harness APIs require paired permissions on both the harness ARN and the underlying AgentCore Runtime (and Memory) resource — e.g. `InvokeHarness` needs both `bedrock-agentcore:InvokeHarness` and `bedrock-agentcore:InvokeAgentRuntime`. A distinct `arn:aws:bedrock-agentcore:<region>:<account>:harness/<id>/harness-endpoint/<name>` resource type exists with its own Create/Update/Delete/Get/List actions. Source: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock-agentcore/latest/devguide/harness-security.html

platforms.name: Cognition Devin Desktop (tier: watching)
details: **v3.10.35 (2026-09-24): MCP servers advertised by ACP clients are now usable inside Devin sessions.** An MCP server the user never configured in Devin can now be reached by a Devin agent because a connected ACP (Agent Client Protocol) client exposes it. Source: https://docs.devin.ai/desktop/changelog

findings.title: Cursor Rollouts — an AI agent with production deploy, telemetry and revert authority
findings.description: A new Cursor bot that attaches to every PR, ingests the customer's production logs, metrics and traces via Datadog/Grafana/Honeycomb integrations, and can autonomously open revert PRs or delegate a fix to a cloud agent. This introduces new inventory entities Zenity does not model: Rollouts monitors (one per PR), per-environment change-health verdicts, CD-system connections, and telemetry-provider connections. The toxic combination is concrete — an agent holding simultaneous read access to production observability data and write access to the source repository, able to revert code with no human in the loop depending on configuration. AISPM must discover Rollouts enablement per org, enumerate its connected deploy and telemetry providers, and flag configurations where autonomous revert is enabled

findings.title: Cursor Security Agents — Security Reviewer and Vulnerability Scanner
findings.description: A new agent family that reads every pull request *in the context of the entire codebase* and, via the Vulnerability Scanner, scans the codebase at rest. New inventory entities: Security Reviewer agent configurations, per-repository enablement, custom codebase rules, and at-rest scan results. The security-relevant property is that these agents ingest whole-repository content — including secrets they are explicitly tasked with finding — and emit findings into PR comments, creating a new data-flow path out of the codebase. AISPM must inventory which repositories have security agents enabled and what custom rules are attached

findings.title: AgentCore harness accepts unvalidated model configuration and caller-supplied skill sources
findings.description: AWS documents that `additionalParams`, `apiBase` and `modelId` on `InvokeHarness` are passed to the model provider without validation. A caller can use LiteLLM's `aws_bedrock_runtime_endpoint` to redirect the signed request — **including the SigV4 signature and session credentials** — to an attacker-chosen endpoint, use OpenAI's `extra_headers` to override the `Authorization` header, attempt role escalation via `aws_role_name` + `sts:AssumeRole`, or redirect inference to a different model, region or provider entirely. Separately, the `skills` field can be overridden per invocation to fetch arbitrary markdown and scripts from any S3 bucket or Git repo, which the harness injects into agent context as trusted instructions. Both are first-class prompt-injection and credential-exfiltration vectors reachable by any principal that passes the IAM/JWT gate. AIRT should add probes for `additionalParams` endpoint redirection and per-invocation skill-source override; AISPM should flag harnesses whose execution role grants `sts:AssumeRole` or whose application forwards caller-supplied `model` and `skills` fields

findings.title: AgentCore `harness-endpoint` resource type and paired-permission IAM model
findings.description: A distinct resource type `arn:aws:bedrock-agentcore:<region>:<account>:harness/<id>/harness-endpoint/<endpointName>` exists with its own `CreateHarnessEndpoint` / `UpdateHarnessEndpoint` / `DeleteHarnessEndpoint` / `GetHarnessEndpoint` / `ListHarnessEndpoints` actions, plus `ListHarnessVersions`. Harness control-plane calls require paired permissions on the harness *and* the underlying Runtime and Memory resources, meaning a principal appearing to hold only harness permissions may in fact carry Runtime and Memory authority. Zenity's AgentCore inventory must add `harness-endpoint` as an entity and model the paired-permission expansion when computing effective agent privilege. Note also that SigV4 callers do **not** get per-user identity propagation into downstream tool calls — only inbound OAuth (Bearer JWT) does — so any SigV4-invoked harness runs downstream tools under a shared service identity

findings.title: Gemini Enterprise D&B Finance Analytics data store with write actions
findings.description: New Public Preview connector giving agents natural-language access to company and credit reports, scores, filings and corporate ownership, and — critically — **write actions** that create and process credit applications and manage folders. New inventory entities: the D&B Finance Analytics data store, its connector-action set, and the credit-application objects it can create. An agent with this connector can originate financial transactions, not merely read reference data. AISPM must discover the data store and enumerate its granted actions. **Doc gap:** Google has published no per-store page for either D&B store; the shared D&B connector overview does not enumerate actions, auth model or entity types, so the action set needs a follow-up sweep once documentation lands

findings.title: Devin Desktop exposes ACP-client MCP servers inside agent sessions
findings.description: As of v3.10.35, MCP servers advertised by a connected ACP (Agent Client Protocol) client are usable from within Devin Desktop sessions. This is a transitive MCP-tool surface: a local agent gains tools that were never registered in Devin's own configuration, so an endpoint inventory built from Devin's MCP config alone will under-report the agent's real tool set. ENDPOINT coverage must resolve MCP servers reachable through ACP clients, not only those declared locally

platforms.name: Claude Enterprise (Anthropic)
details: **Inline tool definitions — `tool_addition` by value (`inline-tools-2026-09-15` beta, September 22)** — a `tool_addition` block in a mid-conversation `role: "system"` message can now carry a **full tool definition by value** (name, description, `input_schema`) rather than naming a tool that was already declared in the request's `tools` array. The `tools` array never changes, so the prompt cache still hits. Re-sending a definition under the same name **replaces the tool's schema from that point onward**. Combined with the `mcp-client-2026-09-15` beta header, the same block can attach an **`mcp_toolset`** mid-conversation, and the response then carries `mcp_tool_listing` blocks enumerating that server's tools. Limits: 10,000 deferred tools, 10,000 tools defined after the first user message, 4 MB of post-first-user-message tool definitions. Computer-use tools cannot be defined inline. Supported on Claude Fable 5.1, Mythos 5.1, Opus 5, Opus 5.5 — on the Claude API, Amazon Bedrock and Google Cloud. Source: https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/mid-conversation-system-messages

**Claude Opus 5.5 (September 22)** — `claude-opus-5-5`, 1M context, 128k max output, always-on adaptive thinking; `thinking: {"type":"disabled"}` and `tool_choice` `any`/`tool` return 400. Computer use requires the `computer_toolset_20260801` toolset. Fast mode available as a research preview. *Model-inventory watchlist item; not raised as a coverage finding.* Source: https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/release-notes/api

platforms.name: Amazon Bedrock AgentCore
details: **Harness: Interactive shells (terminals)** — `InvokeAgentRuntimeCommandShell` opens a persistent, interactive **Bash PTY over WebSocket** inside the microVM running a harness session, at `wss://bedrock-agentcore.<region>.amazonaws.com/runtimes/<harness-arn>/ws/shells`. Environment variables, working directory, command history and running processes persist across inputs. A client can detach and **reconnect with the stored `shellId`**, replaying up to 256 KB of buffered output; up to **10 concurrent shells** per harness session (20 retained active+detached entries), 1-hour connection cap, 64 KB frames, 250 frames/sec. Auth is SigV4 (`bedrock-agentcore:InvokeAgentRuntimeCommandShell`), a SigV4 pre-signed URL, or a bearer token accepted by the harness inbound authorizer — including a **browser-friendly base64url bearer token passed through `Sec-WebSocket-Protocol`**. Works in the managed default environment and in a configured custom container. AWS's own guidance: the shell "can access customer-provided data, files, and secrets in the selected environment or on mounted filesystems" and "connect to network destinations that the session can reach." **CloudTrail records the API call and CloudWatch gets connection metadata, but neither logs terminal input or output.** Source: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock-agentcore/latest/devguide/harness-command-shell.html

platforms.name: ChatGPT Enterprise (OpenAI)
details: **Codex CLI 0.156.0 (September 22)** — fullscreen TUI with search; **voice conversations enabled by default with bundled runtimes**; a **usage analytics dashboard at `/usage`** with plan history tracking; **daemon update management via `/daemon`**; worktree session filtering; **Windows sandbox changes — network policy support, DNS resolution, account handling, and integration with managed proxy routing**; **MCP policy consistency enforcement** and improved MCP credential handling; Code Mode tool metadata improvements and filesystem accessor bindings; refactored Guardian reviewer lifecycle; Mermaid/equation rendering. Source: https://learn.chatgpt.com/docs/changelog

**GPT-6 Sol and GPT-6 Luna (September 22)** — new models in the API, Codex and ChatGPT Work, at ~50% lower API pricing than GPT-5.6; selectable from the Codex model picker as of CLI 0.156.1 (September 23). Follows GPT-6 Astra, already on the watchlist from the 2026-09-18 report. *Model-inventory watchlist item; not raised as a coverage finding.* Source: https://learn.chatgpt.com/docs/changelog

platforms.name: Google Gemini Enterprise
details: **D&B Risk Analytics data store — GA (September 22)** — a second Dun & Bradstreet federated data store alongside D&B Commercial Graph, targeted at KYB onboarding, counterparty due diligence, sanctions screening and risk assessment. It is a **connector with actions**, not a read-only index; Google's own guidance is to associate only one data store with the actions belonging to a single connector type. Available in `global`, `us` and `eu`; VPC Service Controls enforcement requires deleting and recreating existing data stores. Source: https://docs.cloud.google.com/gemini/enterprise/docs/connectors/d-and-b-commercial-graph

findings.title: Anthropic inline tool definitions — tools and MCP servers introduced mid-conversation, by value
findings.description: A `tool_addition` block in a `role: "system"` message can now carry a complete tool definition, so a tool that Claude will call **need never appear in the request's `tools` array**. Every static analysis Zenity performs that reads an agent's declared toolset from the top of the request is now incomplete by design: the real tool surface is the union of `tools` plus every inline definition appended across the conversation, and a later definition under the same name **silently replaces the earlier schema**. Two consequences compound this. First, the same mechanism can attach an entire **`mcp_toolset` mid-conversation** (with `mcp-client-2026-09-15`), which means an MCP server — and the arbitrary tool list it returns in `mcp_tool_listing` — can enter an agent's reach after the conversation started and after any pre-flight policy check ran. Second, because the system-message block is *appended data*, an agent pipeline that builds messages from retrieved or user-influenced content gives an injection a route to **define its own tool** rather than merely persuade the model to misuse an existing one. AIRT needs probes for inline tool injection and mid-conversation MCP attachment; AISPM must treat an agent's tool inventory as conversation-scoped and evolving, parse `tool_addition` and `mcp_tool_listing` blocks as first-class inventory events, and alert on schema replacement of an already-known tool name

findings.title: AgentCore harness interactive shells (`InvokeAgentRuntimeCommandShell`)
findings.description: A new WebSocket API that gives a caller a persistent, stateful Bash terminal inside the microVM running a harness agent — the same environment as the agent, with the same filesystem, mounted secrets and network reachability. AWS states plainly that **terminal input and output are not logged**: CloudTrail captures only the fact of the `InvokeAgentRuntimeCommandShell` call (caller identity, timestamp, source IP, resolved runtime, response status), and CloudWatch receives connection metadata only. Everything typed and everything returned is invisible to AWS-native logging, which makes this the least-observed execution path AgentCore has shipped. Detach-and-reconnect (`shellId` + runtime session ID) means a process started in one connection keeps running unattended and can be resumed later from a different client, and the browser-oriented **base64url bearer token over `Sec-WebSocket-Protocol`** path means a shell can be opened from a browser without SigV4 at all, authorised only by the harness inbound authorizer. Zenity must inventory which principals hold `bedrock-agentcore:InvokeAgentRuntimeCommandShell` and on which harness ARNs, treat any grant of it as a high-privilege finding (AWS's own security note says to restrict it to trusted principals and specific harness ARNs), surface harnesses whose inbound authorizer would accept a bearer-token shell connection, and ingest the CloudTrail event as an AIDR activity type — with the explicit caveat that content-level detection is not available and the compensating control has to be authorisation, not inspection

findings.title: Codex CLI 0.156.0 — always-on voice with bundled runtimes, a local usage dashboard, and managed proxy routing in the Windows sandbox
findings.description: Three changes alter what Codex is on a workstation. **Voice conversations are now enabled by default and ship with bundled runtimes**, which turns the local coding agent into a always-available microphone-driven input path with its own embedded speech runtime on disk — a new prompt-entry vector that leaves no text artifact and a new bundled binary to inventory. The **`/usage` analytics dashboard with plan history** is a locally reachable record of the agent's own consumption; useful as telemetry, and also a reconnaissance surface. The Windows sandbox now carries **network policy support, DNS resolution and integration with managed proxy routing**, meaning Codex's egress on Windows is governed by a configurable local policy object that ENDPOINT should read and assess rather than assume. Alongside these, **MCP policy consistency enforcement** and improved MCP credential handling change how locally configured MCP servers are admitted, and **Code Mode tool metadata plus filesystem accessor bindings** expand what the agent can reach on the filesystem. This is an extension of the Codex daemon/worktree endpoint object already reported 2026-09-18, not a new product, hence MEDIUM

findings.title: Gemini Enterprise D&B Risk Analytics data store (GA)
findings.description: A second Dun & Bradstreet connector reaches GA, and unlike a plain search index it is a **connector with actions** — meaning a Gemini Enterprise agent can invoke operations against an external commercial-risk service, not merely read from it. The declared use cases (KYB onboarding, counterparty due diligence, sanctions screening, risk decisioning) put it directly in a regulated decision path: an agent grounded on this store is producing outputs that feed onboarding and credit decisions, and the store itself becomes a route by which internal counterparty identifiers leave the tenant for a third-party data provider. AISPM must add D&B Risk Analytics as an inventory entity alongside D&B Commercial Graph, enumerate the actions registered for it (the action set is the privilege, not the connector), capture its region binding (`global`/`us`/`eu`) as a data-residency attribute, and flag agents that hold it as a grounding source in a compliance-relevant workflow

platforms.name: Amazon Bedrock AgentCore
details: **Harness: Lifecycle hooks** — hooks fire at `before_invocation`, `before_tool_call`, `after_tool_call` and `after_invocation`, including for inline-function tool calls. An AWS Lambda target returns a synchronous `allow` or `deny` that can stop an invocation or skip a tool call; Amazon SNS and Amazon EventBridge targets receive non-blocking notifications. `InvokeHarness` emits a `hookEvent` for each configured hook that fires. Source: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock-agentcore/latest/devguide/harness-lifecycle-hooks.html

**Harness: Custom OpenAI-compatible endpoints** — OpenAI model configurations now accept an optional `apiBase` field, routing direct OpenAI requests through a customer-specified gateway, proxy, self-hosted endpoint or regional endpoint. Source: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock-agentcore/latest/devguide/harness-models.html

platforms.name: Claude Enterprise (Anthropic)
details: **Life Sciences Verification Program (September 17, 2026)** — a vetting-gated entitlement that replaces an organisation's biology-related safety classifiers with a more permissive set. Two tiers: *Standard Use* (Mythos, Opus and Sonnet with classifiers tuned permissive for science tasks) and *High-risk Use*, an add-on that **removes all safeguards blocking life-sciences requests** for a named project. Cyber classifiers and other safeguards are retained. Grants are annual (Standard) or bi-annual (High-risk), scoped to declared use cases, and enforcement shifts from real-time blocking to offline pattern analysis. Source: https://www.anthropic.com/news/life-sciences-verification-program

platforms.name: Google Gemini Enterprise
details: **Transfer agent ownership (September 21, 2026)** — administrators holding `roles/discoveryengine.agentspaceAdmin` or `roles/discoveryengine.admin` can reassign ownership of a shared agent to another user, including themselves. Shared agents only; the new owner becomes sole owner and the previous owner is downgraded to `agentUser`. Targets may be Google accounts or Workforce Identity Federation principals. Any schedule or event trigger on the agent is marked disabled by the transfer and must be re-enabled by the new owner. Source: https://docs.cloud.google.com/gemini/enterprise/docs/share-custom-agents

findings.title: AgentCore harness lifecycle hooks
findings.description: A new synchronous interception and control surface inside the AgentCore agent loop. Four hook points (`before_invocation`, `before_tool_call`, `after_tool_call`, `after_invocation`) can each bind a Lambda that returns `allow`/`deny` and can halt an invocation or suppress a tool call, plus SNS/EventBridge fan-out targets. This introduces new inventory entities (harness hook configurations, their Lambda/SNS/EventBridge targets) and a new activity type — the `hookEvent` records emitted by `InvokeHarness` — which is a first-class detection feed for what an AgentCore agent actually invoked. It is also a control plane an attacker with harness-config write access can neuter or repurpose: replacing a `deny` Lambda silently removes the customer's own tool-call gating, and a `before_tool_call` Lambda sees every tool argument, making it an exfiltration point. Zenity must inventory hook configurations, alert on hooks removed or repointed, and ingest `hookEvent` as an AIDR activity source

findings.title: Anthropic Life Sciences Verification Program — entitlement-based safeguard removal
findings.description: A verified organisation's Claude deployment can run with biology safety classifiers relaxed (Standard Use) or, at the High-risk tier, with all life-sciences-blocking safeguards removed for a named project. Guardrail behaviour is therefore a property of the *entitlement attached to the workspace/API key*, not of the model — the same `claude-mythos-5`/Opus/Sonnet model ID behaves differently for an entitled org, and Anthropic explicitly moves that tier from real-time blocking to offline pattern analysis. Red-team probes that infer safety posture from refusals will pass falsely against an entitled deployment. AIRT needs a bio-domain probe set, and AISPM needs to record the LSVP entitlement and tier as a property of the Anthropic connection so an unexpected High-risk grant is a finding. Directly parallels the Mythos-5 safeguard-lifting pattern already tracked

findings.title: AgentCore harness custom OpenAI endpoint (`apiBase`)
findings.description: OpenAI model configs in the AgentCore harness now take an `apiBase` pointing at any OpenAI-compatible gateway, proxy, self-hosted or regional endpoint. This is a new outbound model-traffic path that leaves AWS-observed inference entirely — every prompt, tool result and completion for that agent can be routed to an arbitrary third-party host set by a single config field, with no code change and no new IAM resource. AISPM must surface `apiBase` per harness configuration, treat a non-default value as an unmonitored data-egress edge, and flag agents whose model traffic bypasses Bedrock

findings.title: Gemini Enterprise agent ownership transfer
findings.description: A new administrative action that reassigns the sole owner of a shared agent, demoting the previous owner to `agentUser`, and that accepts Workforce Identity Federation principals as well as Google accounts. This mutates an inventory relationship Zenity already models (agent → owner) through a path that is not agent creation, so ownership drift will go unobserved unless the transfer is tracked; it is also a plausible privilege-consolidation move — an admin can make themselves the owner of any shared agent in the tenant. The transfer additionally disables the agent's schedule and event triggers, silently changing autonomous-execution posture. AISPM should treat owner change on an existing agent, and trigger-state change caused by it, as distinct monitored events

platforms.name: Google Gemini Enterprise (secondary)
details: **New actions for Microsoft OneDrive, Outlook, SharePoint and Teams data stores (September 18, Public Preview).** Four Microsoft connectors gained write and management operations. OneDrive: copy folder, move file, move folder, rename file, rename folder, **share file or folder**, update file properties. Outlook: create calendar, RSVP to event, update calendar. SharePoint: create list item, discard check-out, get list fields, get list item, list lists, **share resource**, update file properties, update list, update list item, update page. Teams: **add member to channel**, create channel, create chat, create schedule, create time-off entry, update channel, update channel message, update chat, update chat message, update time-off entry. Source: https://docs.cloud.google.com/gemini/enterprise/docs/manage-actions

**Workflow Builder GA (September 3) — previously unreported.** Formerly Agent Designer. A no-code/low-code surface in the Gemini Enterprise web app where **non-admin end users** create chat agents and multi-step workflows from natural-language prompts or a visual flow editor, connect them to data sources, tools and **MCP servers**, schedule recurring executions, and publish and share them with users or groups. Source: https://docs.cloud.google.com/gemini/enterprise/docs/workflow-builder

findings.title: Gemini Enterprise can now write into Microsoft 365 — share OneDrive files, share SharePoint resources, and add members to Teams channels
findings.description: The September 18 preview adds action sets to the Microsoft OneDrive, Outlook, SharePoint and Teams data stores, converting four read connectors into read-write ones. Three of the new actions are permission-mutating rather than content-mutating, and those are the ones that matter: OneDrive **"share file or folder"**, SharePoint **"share resource"**, and Teams **"add member to channel"**. An agent holding these can change who has access to Microsoft 365 data from outside Microsoft's control plane entirely — the grant is made by a Google-side principal acting through a stored connector credential, so it lands in the tenant as a sharing event without a corresponding Entra agent identity, Copilot Studio agent, or Foundry autopilot behind it. Every Microsoft-side agent-governance surface Zenity tracks (Entra Agent ID, Agent 365, Copilot Studio DLP, Defender Security for AI) sees nothing here, because the actor is not a Microsoft agent. The remaining actions broaden the blast radius in ordinary ways worth inventorying: SharePoint list item and page writes, OneDrive file moves and renames, Outlook calendar creation and event RSVP, and a full Teams management set including channel creation, chat creation, message updates and **time-off entry creation** (a Shifts/workforce-data write, which is employee data). AISPM should model connector actions as a first-class capability on each Gemini Enterprise data store — an inventory that records "SharePoint connector: connected" without recording *which action set is enabled* will now understate reach by an order of magnitude — and should flag any data store where sharing-class actions (`share file or folder`, `share resource`, `add member to channel`) are enabled, since those let an agent expand access rather than merely consume it. AIDR should treat Gemini-originated M365 writes as a distinct activity class and correlate the Google-side action against the Microsoft-side audit event, because neither log alone attributes the change to an agent. This is the fourth consecutive scan (2026-08-21, 2026-08-30, 2026-09-02, 2026-09-18) in which Google expanded actions without expanding the connector list; the connector inventory looks static while the capability surface does not

findings.title: Gemini Enterprise Workflow Builder: end users build, schedule and share agents and workflows with MCP server connections — GA'd September 3, missed on the last scan
findings.description: Workflow Builder (formerly Agent Designer) reached general availability as "an interactive no-code, low-code platform for creating, managing, and turning on chat agents and workflows in your Gemini Enterprise web app." Four properties make it an inventory requirement rather than a UI change. **First, the builder is not admin-gated.** Google's own framing is that it "empowers employees and non-admin users to build and deploy chat agents and workflows" — the constraint is that available tools are "limited to the data connectors, tools, and permissions provisioned by the Gemini Enterprise administrator." That is a real ceiling, but it is a *tenant-wide* ceiling: any connector an admin provisions becomes composable by every end user, so the admin controls the palette and the user controls the composition. Combined with the connector-action finding above, an end user can now assemble a workflow that shares SharePoint resources or adds Teams channel members without any per-workflow review. **Second, workflows connect to MCP servers** — a documented first-class capability, meaning user-authored workflows reach arbitrary external tools through a protocol Zenity already treats as a monitored surface elsewhere. **Third, workflows run on a schedule**, with documented chat-agent execution scheduling. A scheduled workflow is an unattended agent: it acts with no user present, on a recurring cadence, which removes the human-in-the-loop assumption underpinning most interactive-assistant risk models. **Fourth, workflows are publishable and shareable** to specific users or groups, so one user's construction becomes an organizational asset with its own distribution graph. AISPM should discover Workflow Builder chat agents and workflows as inventory entities distinct from Gemini Enterprise's admin-registered agents; record each one's **author** (and whether that author is a non-admin), its connector and tool grants, its MCP server connections, its execution schedule, and its share scope; and flag scheduled workflows holding write-capable or sharing-capable connector actions, workflows connected to MCP servers not on an approved list, and workflows shared organization-wide. This is shadow-agent creation as a shipped product feature, and it pairs directly with the Gemini Enterprise **Projects** entity reported on 2026-09-18 — Projects gives users a self-assembled knowledge base, Workflow Builder gives them a self-assembled actor, and the two are designed to connect. Noting the correction: this GA'd on September 3 and was visible in the release notes read on 2026-09-18, where the adjacent agent-observability item was reported and this one was not

platforms.name: Microsoft Foundry — autopilots (`ms.date` 2026-08-25), missed in the 09-02 pass
details: **Autopilot: a third Foundry agent type defined by holding an Entra agent user account.** "An autopilot is a type of agent that works under its own identity as a persistent, named member of your organization." Every Foundry agent has an Entra **agent identity** (a service principal) from creation; an autopilot additionally has an Entra **agent user account** (a user object) carrying "its own email, calendar, OneDrive, Teams presence, and a place in the organization chart," plus a **manager** who answers for it. Microsoft's three-type table: **Assistive** (agent identity + signed-in user context, acts within that user's permissions), **Background service** (agent identity only, app-only permissions, cannot perform M365 actions), **Autopilot** (agent identity **and** agent user account, acts as itself in M365 including group chats). Source: https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/foundry/agents/concepts/autopilot-overview

**Blueprint-to-instance fan-out.** "You don't build an autopilot. You build a blueprint that teams use to create their own autopilot instances, each with its own identity and its own team-scoped access." One blueprint → many hired instances, each with **its own agent identity and its own agent user account**. Policy is a separate layer: "Configure policy once and every instance inherits it. Update the blueprint and every instance updates. Block the blueprint and every instance stops." Only **Foundry hosted agents** can be published as autopilot blueprints. Three patterns: **group**, **company-wide**, and **personal** autopilots. Source: same

**Explicit tool-versus-data separation.** "Holding a tool isn't the same as holding access to the data behind it. Giving an autopilot a SharePoint tool doesn't give it any SharePoint site, and giving it a mailbox doesn't give it the ability to send mail." Source: same
*(Also in the same August batch and still held as extensions: agent optimizer cost/token accounting, autopilot lifecycle, human-in-the-loop approval steps, toolbox network isolation.)*

platforms.name: Claude Enterprise (Anthropic) — September 3 to September 18
details: **`ant apply` — infrastructure-as-code for agent fleets (CLI ≥ 1.30.0, September 3).** Creates and updates **agents, environments, skills, memory stores and deployments** from files in a repository. Agents are Markdown (frontmatter = config, body = system prompt); environments and memory stores are YAML; deployments are Markdown whose prose "becomes the message that starts each session"; a skill is a directory with `SKILL.md` uploaded as one bundle. Kind is inferred from a `type` field, the containing directory (`agents/`, `environments/`, `memory_stores/`, `deployments/`), or a filename prefix. Resources reference each other **by relative path** and `ant apply` resolves them in dependency order. **A skill reference can be a GitHub URL** (`https://github.com/<owner>/<repo>/tree/<branch>/<dir>`) that `ant apply` downloads and uploads, pinned to the resolved commit until `--upgrade`. State lives in a committed **`claude-lock.json`** recording each resource's kind, ID, version and two hashes (what was sent, what the API returned) plus the bound `organization_id` and `workspace_id`. CI guidance is `ant apply --yes .` on the default branch, authenticated with **Workload Identity Federation**, and the command "refuses credentials that resolve to any other organization or workspace." `--force` overwrites out-of-band edits; `--prune` archives resources whose files were deleted. Source: https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/cli-sdks-libraries/cli/apply

**`auto` permission policy — server-side per-call tool authorization (September 10).** A third policy alongside `always_allow` and `always_ask`. "The server evaluates each call before it runs… Because the evaluation considers the tool, the call's input, and the session's content up to that point, the server can treat two calls to the same tool differently." Three outcomes: the call runs; the call is **denied** (the agent gets `Permission to use {tool_name} has been denied.` with `is_error: true`, and "your client cannot override the denial"); or the call **pauses** for approval. Defaults are unchanged — agent toolset `always_allow`, MCP toolsets `always_ask`, and "no toolset uses `auto` by default." Anthropic's own warning: "`auto` is not a human checkpoint. If the server determines that a call is safe, the call runs before anyone sees it, and its effects might not be reversible." Source: https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/managed-agents/permission-policies

**New event fields on every tool call.** Under **any** policy, `agent.tool_use` and `agent.mcp_tool_use` events now carry **`evaluated_permission`** (`"allow"` / `"ask"` / `"deny"`) and, in most cases, an **`evaluation`** object whose `type` names the resolving policy; under `auto` it nests the server's determination plus a **`reason_code`** (`high_risk`, `indeterminate`). `evaluation` is **absent** when the agent names a tool that isn't enabled (denied without policy evaluation) and on events recorded before the field existed. `agent.custom_tool_use` carries neither field. Source: same

**`ant beta:sessions connect` (September 10)** — attaches a terminal to a running Managed Agents session, shows waiting tool calls and sends the `user.tool_confirmation` event interactively; `--web` serves a session viewer locally. Source: https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/cli-sdks-libraries/cli/sessions-connect

**Compact-on-demand (beta, September 14)** — a top-level **`compaction`** parameter on the Messages API under the `compact-2026-09-04` beta header. The API returns a **signed `compaction` block** summarizing prior messages, and can "keep recent turns word-for-word while preserving thinking validity." Source: https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/compaction

**Compliance API: Claude in Chrome sessions (beta, September 18).** The local session endpoints now return transcripts with **`product_surface: claude_in_chrome`**. The covered surface list is now **Cowork, Claude Code, Claude Science, Claude for Microsoft 365, and Claude in Chrome**; Cowork and Claude Code are stable, the other three are beta. No new key, scope, setting or client update is required — the existing Compliance Access Key with `read:compliance_user_data` works. Source: https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/manage-claude/compliance-sessions

platforms.name: Amazon Bedrock AgentCore — September release notes
details: **Consent Portal for AgentCore Identity.** "A consent portal is a hosted, AWS-managed portal that authenticates your end users to an OpenID Connect (OIDC) identity provider (IdP) and gathers their consent before your agent accesses a downstream resource on their behalf." Each portal **attaches to a single AgentCore Gateway** (its source) and uses an **OAuth2 credential provider** referencing the same IdP the gateway's inbound JWT authorizer trusts. The gateway must use **JWT inbound authentication** and the IdP's permitted scopes must include `openid`. You direct users to the portal's **`portalUrl`**. "The portal keeps the OAuth flow server-side: the browser never holds a token." Managed with **create, get, list, update and delete consent-portal operations**, plus a **consent portal execution role** and configurable **consent portal targets**. Sources: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock-agentcore/latest/devguide/identity-consent-portal.html and https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock-agentcore/latest/devguide/release-notes.html

**Evaluations: TypeScript agent framework support** — AgentCore Evaluations now evaluates agents built with the TypeScript versions of Strands Agents, LangGraph and OpenAI Agents, plus the **Vercel AI SDK** (TypeScript-only). Held as an extension of the already-reported evaluations surface, but note the Vercel AI SDK is a framework this monitor has not previously seen named in an AWS evaluation scope. Source: same

findings.title: Microsoft Foundry autopilots are agents that hold a real Entra *user* account — mailbox, calendar, OneDrive, Teams presence and a manager — and one blueprint fans out into an unbounded set of them
findings.description: Foundry now documents a **third agent type** whose definition is identity, not capability. "An autopilot is a type of agent that works under its own identity as a persistent, named member of your organization. It holds a standing role rather than answering one request at a time." Every Foundry agent already carries an Entra **agent identity** (a service principal). What makes an autopilot different is that it **also** carries an Entra **agent user account** — a *user object* — and Microsoft enumerates exactly what that buys: "its own email, calendar, OneDrive, Teams presence, and a place in the organization chart," plus the ability to "perform Microsoft 365 actions **as itself**." Microsoft states the test plainly: "An agent either has its own agent user account or it doesn't, which is what makes identity a reliable definition. The distinction between an agent and an autopilot is **binary**." **This collapses the boundary Zenity's M365 and Entra collectors rely on.** An autopilot appears in the tenant's user object space, in the org chart, and in mail and Teams traffic as a named member of staff; it can act in **group chats** where no single user's permissions apply; and it "can act without being prompted" in response to events with **no user in the loop at all** — which is precisely the scenario Microsoft says motivated the feature. Any inventory, DLP rule, sharing-risk calculation or anomaly baseline that partitions principals into "humans" and "service principals" will now classify autopilots on the wrong side of the line. **The fan-out is the second half of the finding.** "You don't build an autopilot. You build a blueprint that teams use to create their own autopilot instances, each with its own identity and its own team-scoped access." A regular Foundry agent is one-to-one — one agent, one blueprint, one agent identity, no user account. An autopilot blueprint is **one-to-many**: one blueprint, many *hired* instances, and **each instance gets its own agent identity *and* its own agent user account**. So a single reviewed, approved object silently becomes N mailbox-holding principals with N different access grants, each scoped by whichever manager hired it. Microsoft's own argument for the design is that it prevents ten teams from building ten near-identical agents whose "controls drift apart," and that argument is sound — but the inventory consequence is that **the governed object and the acting principal are different objects at different cardinalities**, and only the blueprint is centrally reviewed. Three specifics are directly actionable. **First, the blueprint is the kill switch**: "Update the blueprint and every instance updates. Block the blueprint and every instance stops." AISPM should model the blueprint→instance relationship as a first-class inventory edge, because it is simultaneously the blast radius of a bad change and the only single point of containment. **Second, only Foundry *hosted* agents can be published as autopilot blueprints**, which ties this directly to the hosted-agent surface already tracked — including the **bring-your-own-registry** path reported on 2026-09-02, meaning an autopilot's container image can originate outside Azure entirely. **Third, Microsoft draws a tool/data distinction Zenity should adopt verbatim as a rule**: "Holding a tool isn't the same as holding access to the data behind it. Giving an autopilot a SharePoint tool doesn't give it any SharePoint site, and giving it a mailbox doesn't give it the ability to send mail." Effective reach is therefore the **intersection** of the blueprint's tool grants and the instance's resource grants, and an inventory that reports only one of the two will systematically over- or under-state what an autopilot can do. AISPM should discover autopilot blueprints as an entity distinct from agents, enumerate hired instances per blueprint, resolve each instance's **agent user account** back to its Entra user object and its **manager**, join that user object against mailbox, OneDrive, Teams and SharePoint permission grants the same way it would for a human, and flag: an autopilot user account with no manager assigned; an instance whose resource grants exceed its sibling instances from the same blueprint; a **company-wide** autopilot (Microsoft's own pattern for "one production instance per business process") holding tenant-wide scope; and a **personal** autopilot created by a single user outside any review. AIDR should treat activity from an agent user account as agent activity, not human activity, wherever the two are currently conflated. Note the correction: these pages were published in the August Foundry roll-up and were in the material this monitor held back on 2026-09-02 without reading

findings.title: Anthropic moved per-call tool authorization onto its own server, added a decision record to every tool event, and documented the prompt-injection path into it
findings.description: The new **`auto` permission policy** (September 10, `managed-agents-2026-04-01` beta) is a third option alongside `always_allow` and `always_ask`, and it changes where the authorization decision happens: "the server evaluates each call before it runs. Because the evaluation considers the tool, the call's input, and the session's content up to that point, **the server can treat two calls to the same tool differently**." Three outcomes — run, **deny**, or pause for approval — and the denial is final: the agent receives `Permission to use {tool_name} has been denied.` with `is_error: true`, and "**your client cannot override the denial**." Sending a `user.tool_confirmation` for a server-denied call is rejected with a 400. **Three things follow for Zenity.** **First, there is now a decision record on every tool call, under every policy.** `agent.tool_use` and `agent.mcp_tool_use` events carry **`evaluated_permission`** (`"allow"` / `"ask"` / `"deny"`) and, in most cases, an **`evaluation`** object naming the resolving policy; under `auto` it nests the server's determination and a **`reason_code`** of `high_risk` or `indeterminate`. This is a genuinely new, free, first-party detection signal — **a `deny` with `reason_code: high_risk` is Anthropic telling you an agent tried something its own classifier judged dangerous**, and AIDR should ingest it as a first-class alert rather than as event metadata. Two absence cases must be handled correctly or they will read as gaps: `evaluation` is missing when the agent names a tool that isn't enabled (the server denies without evaluating, so `evaluated_permission: "deny"` with no `evaluation` means *unknown tool*, not *blocked by policy*), and it is missing on events predating the field, which Anthropic says to read as `always_allow` when the outcome is `allow` and `always_ask` when it is `ask`. `agent.custom_tool_use` carries neither field, so **custom tools remain entirely client-authorized and produce no decision record at all** — that is the blind spot in this telemetry and it is where an adversary would put the tool that matters. **Second, `auto` is an injection target and Anthropic says so.** "What you post in `user.message` events counts as your intent, and it can lead the server to allow a call it would otherwise deny." The server "assesses but does not take instructions from" tool results, fetched webpages, MCP responses, or messages between session threads — but `user.message` is trusted, and: "**If you relay untrusted end-user input in `user.message` events, the server reads that input as your intent too, and it can get a call allowed.**" That is an explicit, vendor-documented privilege-escalation path in any application that forwards end-user chat into a Managed Agents session, which is the overwhelmingly common architecture. **AIRT should build this as a probe**: place attacker-controlled text in `user.message`, attempt a tool call the server denies without it, and measure whether the denial flips. **Third, `auto` will be mistaken for a control it is not.** Anthropic's own warning: "`auto` is not a human checkpoint. If the server determines that a call is safe, the call runs before anyone sees it, and its effects might not be reversible." AISPM should inventory the resolved permission policy **per toolset and per tool** (defaults are agent toolset `always_allow`, MCP toolsets `always_ask`, and no toolset uses `auto` by default), flag any agent that **downgraded an MCP toolset from `always_ask` to `always_allow` or `auto`**, flag `auto` on destructive tools such as `bash`, and record that **running sessions keep the toolset configuration they were created with** — so a policy tightening does not take effect on sessions already in flight, and a point-in-time posture read will disagree with live session behavior

findings.title: `ant apply` turns Claude agent fleets into Git-managed infrastructure — including skills pulled straight from GitHub URLs — and the authoritative inventory is now a lockfile in a repository
findings.description: `ant apply` (CLI ≥ 1.30.0, September 3) "creates and updates Claude API resources from files: **agents, environments, skills, memory stores, and deployments**. They live in your repository and change through the same review as your code." This is the Claude platform's answer to Terraform, and it relocates the source of truth for an agent fleet **out of the Anthropic Console and into version control**. Five properties matter. **First, the resource set is the whole attack surface.** An agent file's frontmatter is its configuration and its body is its **system prompt**; an **environment** YAML declares the sandbox including `networking: {type: unrestricted}`; a **memory store** YAML declares persistent cross-session state; a **deployment** Markdown carries a **cron schedule** and prose that "becomes the message that starts each session" — i.e. **an unattended, recurring agent trigger defined in a text file**. Every one of these is an entity Zenity already models, and all of them now change by pull request. **Second, skills can be pulled from arbitrary GitHub URLs.** A skill reference may be `https://github.com/<owner>/<repo>/tree/<branch>/<dir>`, which `ant apply` "downloads and uploads," pinned to the resolved commit **until you run with `--upgrade`** (with `GITHUB_TOKEN` for private repositories). That is a third-party supply-chain edge into an agent's capability set, expressed as one line of YAML, and the pinning is only as good as the discipline around `--upgrade`. This is the [[agent-plugins-cross-vendor-standard]] pattern again: capability arriving from a repository rather than from a platform control plane. **Third, `claude-lock.json` is the inventory artifact and it is committed to the repo.** It records, per file, the resource `kind`, its API `id`, its `version`, and **two hashes** — `hash` (what was last sent) and `remote_hash` (what the API returned) — plus the bound `organization_id` and `workspace_id`. Zenity should read this file directly: it is a complete, machine-readable manifest of an organization's declared agents, and the hash pair is a **drift detector** — a mismatch means a resource was changed outside the files, which `ant apply` refuses to overwrite without `--force`. AISPM should treat the presence of `--force` in a CI pipeline as a finding, because it means declared state is being pushed over out-of-band changes without review. **Fourth, CI runs under Workload Identity Federation.** Anthropic recommends `ant apply --yes .` on the default branch after merge, authenticated by WIF rather than a stored key, and the command "refuses credentials that resolve to any other organization or workspace." Good design — and it means **a CI identity now holds create-and-update rights over an organization's entire agent fleet**, which AISPM should enumerate as a privileged non-human principal alongside the personal and service-account keys reported on 2026-09-02. **Fifth, the adoption gap is real and detectable**: `ant apply` "can't adopt a resource you created in the Console or with `ant beta:agents create`," and applying a file describing an existing agent **creates a second one**. So organizations mid-migration will have duplicate agents, and only the lockfile-tracked half is governed by code review. AISPM should discover `claude-lock.json` files in customer repositories, parse them into agent/environment/memory-store/deployment inventory, reconcile that list against the Admin API's live resource list in **both directions** (lockfile-but-not-live = pruned or stale; live-but-not-lockfile = Console-created and outside code review), flag deployments carrying cron schedules as unattended triggers, flag environments with unrestricted networking, resolve every GitHub-URL skill reference to its pinned commit and the repository's ownership, and alert when `--prune` would archive a resource

findings.title: ServiceNow Zurich is GA with a Build Agent that writes apps into the global scope and an AI Control Tower that publishes managed agents to external registries
findings.description: The Zurich release family reached GA (highlights page updated **2026-08-07**) and it is the most agent-dense ServiceNow release this monitor has seen. Four items, each a distinct coverage gap. **First, "publishing managed agents to external registries" — zero hits across every prior report.** This is the outbound complement to two edges already recorded: the ServiceNow→**Microsoft Agent 365** publication path found on 2026-09-02, and Agent 365's own auto-ingest of Bedrock and Vertex agents found on 2026-08-30. ServiceNow is now a **general-purpose agent publisher** into other vendors' registries, which means a ServiceNow-authored agent can appear in a customer's AWS, Microsoft or Google agent inventory as a native record while its logic, its tool grants and its lifecycle remain in ServiceNow. AISPM must model registry publication as an inventory **edge** and must not count the source and the published copy as two agents; more importantly it must determine **which platform is authoritative** for the agent's permissions, because the registry record will show the destination platform's view and the destination platform cannot revoke what ServiceNow granted. **Second, Build Agent creates applications in the *global scope*.** Build Agent generates ServiceNow applications from natural-language prompts inside ServiceNow Studio, and Zurich adds "the ability to create apps and newly supported metadata **in the global scope**" plus "additional **Model Context Protocol (MCP)** support." Scoped applications are ServiceNow's isolation primitive; **global scope is the absence of it**. An LLM-driven app generator that can write global-scope metadata is a privilege-escalation surface inside the Now Platform itself, and the MCP support means that generator can reach external tools while doing it. AIRT should treat natural-language app generation into global scope as a prompt-injection target with platform-wide consequences, and AISPM should inventory Build Agent-generated applications by scope, flagging every global-scope artifact. **Third, Machine Identity Access Controls** — "Enforce access to data via REST or SOAP endpoints" — is ServiceNow shipping first-party non-human-identity authorization, which is both an ingestion source (it is a permission model Zenity can read) and a competitive overlap. **Fourth, the redesigned AI Control Tower** adds **automated deduplication** of redundant AI assets, **AI Service Graph Connectors** discovering assets across AWS, Microsoft and GCP, and **kill switch** containment for rogue agents. The dedup logic is the one to watch: an inventory that silently merges records it believes are duplicates will disagree with Zenity's counts, and the merge criteria are undocumented. AISPM should ingest AI Control Tower's asset graph where a customer runs it, reconcile it against Zenity's own discovery, and treat a Control Tower dedup as a hypothesis to verify rather than a fact. **Source caveat, unchanged for five scans**: the family index at `servicenow.com/docs/r/release-notes/family-release-notes.html` — the URL in `sources.json` — asserts no feature content; the productive page is the Zurich highlights roll-up

findings.title: AgentCore added an AWS-hosted consent portal — a new delegation surface where end users grant agents access to their resources, with its own resource type and CRUD API
findings.description: The **Consent Portal** (September) is "a hosted, AWS-managed portal that authenticates your end users to an OpenID Connect (OIDC) identity provider (IdP) and **gathers their consent before your agent accesses a downstream resource on their behalf**." It is a new AgentCore Identity resource with **create, get, list, update and delete consent-portal operations**, a dedicated **consent portal execution role**, and configurable **consent portal targets**. Each portal **attaches to exactly one AgentCore Gateway** as its source, requires that gateway to use **JWT inbound authentication**, and uses an **OAuth2 credential provider** referencing the same IdP the gateway's authorizer trusts, whose permitted scopes must include `openid`. Users are directed to the portal's **`portalUrl`**. AWS notes the flow stays server-side: "the browser never holds a token." **Why this matters more than a typical identity feature.** Delegated consent is the mechanism by which an agent acquires a human's authority over a third-party system, and until now AgentCore's consent path was something each builder assembled themselves — meaning it was idiosyncratic, hard to find, and effectively invisible to inventory. A **hosted, named, enumerable resource** changes that in both directions: it gives Zenity an API to enumerate (**which agents can ask which users for which scopes**), and it gives an attacker a **credible, AWS-branded, AWS-hosted URL** to phish with. A consent portal is a consent-grant UI hosted on AWS infrastructure, presented to end users, that results in an autonomous agent holding standing access to their resources — the classic OAuth illicit-consent-grant attack, with the added property that the relying party is a non-human that will use the grant unattended. AISPM should add **consent portals as an inventory entity**, resolve each portal to its **source Gateway** and to the **OAuth2 credential provider and IdP** behind it, enumerate the **scopes** a portal can request and flag any portal requesting scopes broader than its agent's documented purpose, and treat the combination of a consent portal plus a gateway with permissive JWT `AllowedClients`/`AllowedAudience` as a toxic pair — noting that those exact authorizer fields are the ones AWS Agent Registry **does not carry into its records** (recorded 2026-09-02), so a registry-derived view cannot evaluate this pairing and Zenity's must read the gateway directly. AIDR should model consent grants and revocations through a portal as activity, since a grant is the moment an agent's effective reach expands and there is otherwise no tool-configuration change to observe. AIRT should probe whether a portal's `portalUrl` can be reached and presented out of context, and whether the consent screen names the agent in a way an end user could verify

findings.title: The Claude Compliance API now returns Claude in Chrome session transcripts — a browser-resident agent surface Zenity has never collected
findings.description: As of **September 18**, the Compliance API's **local** session endpoints return transcripts of **Claude in Chrome** sessions under **`product_surface: claude_in_chrome`**, in beta for Claude Enterprise organizations. The covered surface list is now **Cowork, Claude Code, Claude Science, Claude for Microsoft 365, and Claude in Chrome** — with Cowork and Claude Code stable and the other three in beta. No new key, scope, setting or client update is required: the existing **Compliance Access Key** with **`read:compliance_user_data`** works, so any Zenity deployment already collecting Claude Code and Cowork transcripts can extend to this surface with a parameter change and no customer action. **The significance is the surface, not the endpoint.** A browser-resident Claude agent operates inside the user's authenticated web sessions — every SaaS application the user is logged into, with the user's cookies, in the user's tab. Its transcript is therefore a record of agent activity against systems that have **no server-side agent integration at all** and would appear in those systems' logs as ordinary user activity. This is the closest thing available to ground truth for browser-agent behavior, and it is the natural counterpart to the Claude for M365 office-agents surface recorded in [[claude-office-agents-coverage-gap]]. AIDR should add `claude_in_chrome` to the local-session collection set, model browser-agent tool calls as a distinct activity type (the transcript is "the sequence of user prompts, assistant responses, and **tool calls and results**"), and correlate browser-agent sessions against the same user's activity in monitored SaaS applications to identify actions that were agent-driven rather than human. AISPM should record which of the five product surfaces a customer's Claude Enterprise organization actually has in use, because each one is a separate endpoint surface with a separate stability tier — and the three beta surfaces are exactly the three newest, meaning collection coverage lags product adoption by design. The documented blind spots recorded in [[anthropic-source-and-coverage-gaps]] continue to double as a coverage map and should be re-read against this expanded surface list

findings.title: Gemini Enterprise Projects is a new user-created knowledge-base entity that blends Drive, SharePoint and local uploads under per-project membership
findings.description: **Projects** (September 4, GA) lets any user "build a dedicated knowledge base for your own work or to collaborate with your team," holding up to **50 files and linked documents** drawn from local uploads (PDF, DOCX, PPTX, XLSX, CSV, HTML, TXT), **Google Drive files and folders**, free-text notes, and **third-party connectors such as Microsoft SharePoint**. This is a new inventory entity with its own membership model, and three of its properties are posture-relevant. **First, the permission model is mixed.** Linking Drive content "doesn't change their original sharing permissions" and members "only see files they have permission to access" — correct, permission-trimmed behavior. But **locally uploaded files are visible and deletable by all members**, which means a project is simultaneously a permission-respecting view over Drive *and* a permission-flattening store for anything uploaded directly. A single object with two different access semantics is exactly where data leaks, and an inventory that records a project's member list without distinguishing linked from uploaded content will misstate exposure. **Second, invited members receive Editor permissions by default** — the default grant is write, not read. **Third, projects are user-created**, so this is shadow-knowledge-base creation as a product feature: a user can assemble corporate SharePoint content, Drive folders and uploaded documents into a durable, shared, agent-groundable corpus with no administrative involvement. AISPM should inventory Gemini Enterprise projects as a data-store entity, record per-project membership and owner, **separate linked content (permission-inherited) from uploaded content (project-flattened)** in exposure calculations, and flag projects containing uploaded files alongside members who would not have had access to the equivalent source documents. Two companion items from the same window: **Google Cloud Marketplace now supports semantic search for agent discovery** (September 8), lowering the friction for a user to find and adopt a third-party agent — a shadow-agent acquisition path worth watching; and **nine new preview connectors landed in three weeks** (CoinDesk, Relativity, Streak, Superhuman Mail on September 4; Campfire, Clay, CourtListener, Daloopa, MSCI on August 28) with **new actions** for AirOps, Airtable and Zoho Desk, continuing the read-to-write expansion pattern reported on 2026-08-21, 2026-08-30 and 2026-09-02 where Google widens what already-connected data stores can *do* without the connector list changing. Sources: https://docs.cloud.google.com/gemini/enterprise/docs/projects and https://docs.cloud.google.com/gemini/enterprise/docs/release-notes

findings.title: Salesforce shipped Koa, a CRM-specific reasoning model trained for tool use, and repositioned the platform as AIforce
findings.description: At Dreamforce (September 15-17) Salesforce announced **Koa**, "Salesforce's first CRM reasoning model," built by post-training **NVIDIA Nemotron 3 Super** on a proprietary synthetic dataset "modeled on enterprise knowledge from nearly three decades of CRM deployments." Salesforce's own framing is the part that matters to Zenity: Koa is "purpose-built to help agents **reason through complex, multistep workflows and use the right tools** to get work done," and its training corpus reflects "the reasoning, **tool use**, and decision-making skills Agentforce agents perform across CRM workflows." No customer data was used in training. **Availability is select pilot customers now in Agentforce, GA expected winter 2026 in U.S. regions.** Three consequences. **First, a new model identifier enters the Agentforce inventory** — AISPM should add Koa to the model watchlist and record which Agentforce agents are configured to use it, because a pilot-gated model in a customer tenant is evidence of an early-access arrangement the customer's own governance may not have reviewed. **Second, a model explicitly optimized for tool selection changes AIRT's assumptions.** Red-team fixtures calibrated against general-purpose models will not predict the behavior of a model post-trained specifically on CRM tool-calling: it will be more willing to chain tool calls, and more confident in selecting them, which raises the value of prompt-injection testing against Agentforce agents rather than lowering it. AIRT should build Koa-specific probes once GA lands and should not assume Agentforce guardrail behavior is model-independent — the lesson from [[claude-mythos-5-safeguards-lifted]] is that guardrail behavior is a property of the deployment. **Third, `AIforce` appears to be a platform-level rebrand** (announced the same day) of the kind that historically breaks Zenity's name-matching in rules, reports and connector labels — the same failure mode as the Vertex→Gemini Enterprise rename in [[vertex-now-gemini-enterprise]] and the Foundry RBAC role rename reported on 2026-09-02. Salesforce documentation had not caught up at scan time: `developer.salesforce.com/docs/ai/agentforce/guide` returns **403** and `salesforce.com/releases/` remains unreachable, so both the model's configuration surface and the rebrand's scope need a follow-up read once the Winter '27 docs publish. Sources: https://www.salesforce.com/news/press-releases/2026/09/15/koa-reasoning-model/ and https://www.salesforce.com/news/

findings.title: Cursor added a coordinator agent that fans out to "thousands of subagents" and self-hosted machines that keep agent tool execution inside the customer's own network
findings.description: Two September releases that together move Cursor from an IDE with an agent into an agent platform with an IDE. **Cursor Projects (September 10)** introduces a **coordinator agent** that "delegates tasks to thousands of subagents in parallel," maintains **shared context across cloud and local machines**, and supports **subscriptions** that monitor Slack channels and run scheduled tasks. Three distinct problems for ENDPOINT. The *cardinality* — an inventory that counts agents per workstation is meaningless against a coordinator that spawns subagents at that scale; the unit of inventory has to become the coordinator and its delegation policy. The *context bridge* — state deliberately spanning cloud and local means a local capture is a partial view by design, and data can traverse the boundary without a file ever landing on disk. And the *triggers* — a subscription watching a Slack channel is an **unattended, externally-triggered agent whose input is attacker-reachable**: anyone who can post in a monitored channel can initiate agent work. AIRT should treat Slack-channel subscriptions as a first-class prompt-injection entry point. **Self-Hosted Machines (September 2)** is the complement: infrastructure for "keeping tool execution within internal networks," with dynamic pool scheduling and autoscaling, **computer use on Linux and Mac with desktop automation**, and integrations spanning AWS Lambda, Coder, Cloudflare, Daytona, Modal, Namespace, Vercel and E2B. Read from a defender's seat this is welcome — execution moves inside the perimeter where it can be observed — but it also means **Cursor agents now run as workloads in the customer's own cloud accounts**, with desktop automation, reachable from a vendor control plane. ENDPOINT and AISPM have to cover this jointly: these are neither endpoint processes nor cloud agents but both. AISPM should discover self-hosted machine pools as agent compute resources, attribute them to the Cursor organization that schedules them, and enumerate the credentials they carry; ENDPOINT should treat a workstation participating in a Project's shared context as holding data whose origin is outside it. Cursor remains **watching** tier, but the last three scans have produced Cursor findings and this pair is a capability jump, not an increment — a tier review is warranted

findings.title: Anthropic's compact-on-demand returns a signed summary block that replaces conversation history the API will never show again
findings.description: **Compact-on-demand** (beta, September 14, `compact-2026-09-04` header) adds a top-level **`compaction`** parameter to the Messages API. The API returns a **signed `compaction` block** summarizing prior messages and "can keep recent turns word-for-word while preserving thinking validity." Operationally this is a context-window management feature and a good one. For monitoring it is **evidence compression at the API boundary**: the turns folded into a compaction block are replaced by a model-authored summary, and anything an investigator would have read in the original — an injected instruction, a tool result, a leaked value, the exact phrasing that preceded a harmful action — survives only insofar as the summarizer chose to carry it. A signed summary is not a transcript. This compounds the **per-tool MCP `output_token_limit`** truncation setting reported on 2026-09-02: the pipeline now has two independent, configurable points at which content is discarded before it reaches anything durable. AIDR should treat the presence of a `compaction` block as a **collection-integrity signal**, flag sessions where compaction occurred so downstream analysis is not read as complete, and — where the Compliance API is the collection path — verify empirically whether compacted turns remain retrievable in exported transcripts or whether the export reflects the compacted view. That question determines whether compaction is a cosmetic concern or a genuine eDiscovery gap, and it should be answered before a customer asks. The block being **signed** is the constructive half: a signature implies verifiable provenance, so AIDR may be able to detect a *forged* or *tampered* compaction block, which is worth confirming with Anthropic

findings.title: Codex CLI added a Windows background daemon with scheduled self-updates, isolated git worktrees, and biometric gating on MCP requests
findings.description: Two releases in nine days materially change what Codex is on a workstation. **0.154.0 (September 9)** added a **Windows background server with daemon lifecycle commands** and experimental **worktree support** for isolated checkouts in new and forked sessions; **0.155.0 (September 17)** added **configurable daemon update schedules with thread recovery after restarts**, **Touch ID verification for MCP requests** on supported Macs, **AWS credential sourcing from configured commands for Amazon Bedrock**, and experimental **voice conversations**. The composite is a **persistent, self-updating background process on Windows and macOS that survives restarts, recovers its agent threads, and holds cloud credentials** — which is a different endpoint object than a CLI a developer invokes. ENDPOINT should discover the Codex daemon as a running service rather than as a foreground process, record its **configured update schedule** (a self-update channel is a supply-chain path, and one whose cadence is now customer-configurable and therefore auditable), and capture thread-recovery state as agent state that persists across reboots. **Worktrees** are the second item: an agent operating in an isolated checkout is working on files that are not the developer's working tree, so a monitor watching the primary checkout sees nothing — ENDPOINT should enumerate git worktrees as agent-reachable filesystem scope. **`AWS credential sourcing from configured commands for Amazon Bedrock`** means Codex now obtains AWS credentials by **executing an arbitrary configured command**, which is both a credential-acquisition path to inventory and a code-execution vector defined in local configuration. The constructive item is **Touch ID verification for MCP requests**: a biometric, per-request human checkpoint in front of MCP tool calls is the strongest local control Codex has shipped, and its *absence* on a machine that supports it is now a detectable posture gap — ENDPOINT should assess whether it is enabled. Also noted: **GPT-6-Astra** is now selectable in Codex and **in Amazon Bedrock catalogs**, a new model identifier for the model-inventory watchlist across both OpenAI and AWS paths

findings.title: Devin Desktop can now drive agents on remote hosts over SSH, always runs ACP, and patched a workspace-trust bypass
findings.description: **v3.10.23 (September 10)** added **Remote Agent Hosts**: connect to agents via **SSH with saved hosts**, status indicators and server icons in the sidebar, with sessions that "recover exact transcripts after reconnect." The desktop application is now a **control console for agents executing on other machines** — the agent's filesystem, network position and credentials are the remote host's, not the workstation's, so an endpoint agent inspecting the local machine will find a UI and a transcript but no execution. ENDPOINT should enumerate **saved SSH hosts** as agent execution targets and treat each as a separate scope requiring its own coverage. The same release made **ACP always enabled** by removing the enable/disable toggle — a protocol surface that was previously optional is now unconditional and should be assumed present on every install — and changed MCP behavior so that **authorization "opens provider directly"** and **Docker-based MCP servers launch correctly**, meaning containerized MCP servers are now a working and therefore likely-to-appear configuration on these endpoints. Separately, **v3.10.31 (September 16)** fixed a real bypass worth recording: "Restricted Mode blocks restricted workspace settings written in **nested object form**, not just the dotted form." Restricted Mode is the workspace-trust boundary, and until this release a restricted setting expressed as a nested object rather than a dotted key **was not blocked** — a straightforward serialization-level bypass of a trust control. ENDPOINT should confirm customers are on ≥ v3.10.31 and should generalize the lesson: workspace-trust controls that match on key *syntax* rather than resolved *configuration* are bypassable by re-encoding, and the same test is worth running against the equivalent controls in Cursor, Kiro and VS Code. Note the source drift confirmed again this scan: `windsurf.com/changelog` 308-redirects to `docs.devin.ai/desktop/changelog`
